4.0 SITE INVESTIGATION AND LABORATORY TEST PROGRAM
2 
This section presents a summary of the existing, current, and planned explorations for the IDF, along with
3 
the laboratory test results for tests conducted during this design effort.
4 
4.1 
Field Explorations
5 
This section discusses the existing and current soil explorations for the IDF. The generalized soil profile
6 
used in the analysis and design is presented; the engineering soil properties used for design are presented
7 
and discussed in Section 5 and related appendices.
8 
4.1.1 
Existing Explorations
9 
Several field explorations have been conducted in the general area of the IDF, as discussed in Section
10 
3.4.1 and presented in Figure 3-1. Figure 1-2 shows the current IDF footprint and the closest borings to
11 
the planned facility. As shown in Figure 1-2, with the exception of one boring, the existing explorations
12 
are all outside of the footprint of the IDF.
13 
The existing field explorations at the IDF site have been conducted primarily for geologic and
14 
hydrogeologic characterization on a "big picture" scale. The existing explorations provide detailed
15 
information for the purposes for which they were conducted; however, from a geotechnical engineering
16 
perspective, the existing borings at or near the IDF site provides only general information, as discussed
17 
below.
18 
Depth of Interest-In many cases, the explorations focused on providing detailed information for the
19 
entire soil column above the bedrock at the IDF site (300 or more feet below ground surface [bgs]). The
20 
primary depth of interest for detailed engineering and design purposes is the depth of the planned cell
21 
excavation (roughly 50 feet below the existing ground surface); for a few analyses, information about the
22 
material 25 to 50 feet below the base of the excavation is also important.
23 
Type of Information-As intended, the existing explorations was generally focused on providing
24 
information for geologic characterization purposes. This focus differs from the key items generally
25 
required for geotechnical design, including Standard Penetration Testing (SPT) per ASTM requirements
26 
and classification by the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) in both the field and the laboratory.
27 
For coarse-grained soils (sands and gravels), that make up the bulk of the native soil profile, in situ SPT
28 
in conjunction with grain-size data is the primary basis for determining geotechnical engineering
29 
parameters of the soil, such as shear strength. In all cases the SPT values were either not readily available
30 
or were conducted with non-standard equipment. Also, the existing grain size data and soil
31 
classifications, both for field and laboratory results were based on the Wentworth scale, which differs
32 
from the USCS scale at the gravel and fines divisions. These are the key division points for classifying
33 
coarse-grained soils. In particular, the break point for fines contents is important in determining the
34 
suitability of the excavated soils for use in the admix liner as well as for other on-site filling purposes.
35 
Many of the soils within the depth of interest for the IDF are near this classification break point.
36 
Proximity to the IDF-As shown in Figure 1-2, in nearly all cases the explorations were located outside
37 
of the IDF footprint. The standard of practice for geotechnical engineering is to place explorations within
38 
or very close to the footprint of the proposed structure, if possible.
39 
There have been several geotechnically focused explorations conducted for various projects at Hanford.
40 
The projects closest and/or most applicable to the IDF site are:
41 
The Grout Vault project, located approximately one-half mile east of the IDF site (Dames and Moore,
42 
1988).
43 
The W-025 Project, a radioactive mixed-waste land disposal facility designed in accordance with RCRA
44 
Subtitle C design criteria, located several miles west of the IDF site (in Area 200W, Golder Associates,
45 
1995, 1994a, 1994b, and 1988).
46 
The RPP-WTP, location approximately 1 mile east of the IDF site (Shannon and Wilson, 2000 and 2001).

5.1 
Slope Stability
5 
Slope stability for the IDF landfill was examined for liner veneer (side slope) stability, earthwork
6 
stability, waste/fill global stability. The analyses for each of these cases are summarized in the sections
7 
below; Appendices C.1.a through C. I.c presents the analyses and results in detail.
8 
5.1.1 
Liner Veneer (Side Slope) Stability
9 
The veneer stability of the liner system on the side slopes was evaluated for the period prior to waste
10 
filling. The analysis examined the potential for sliding of the drainage and operations layers on the liner
11 
system before waste is placed.
12 
The analyses were conducted using the weakest of the interface strengths of the various lining system
13 
components. The interface strengths were determined from regression analyses of data gathered from
14 
various sources, including site-specific test data completed to date. Based on the data (presented in
15 
Appendix C. .a), the critical interface is the textured HDPE/CDN interface. Properties of the cover soil
16 
(operations layer) were determined from laboratory testing to date on the materials expected to be used
17 
for the operations layer.
18 
Four loading conditions were examined:
19 
* 
Dead load: self-weight of the lining system (including the first operations layer)
20 
* 
Dead load + Equipment: self-weight of the lining system with an equipment load
21 
* 
Dead load + Seepage: self-weight of the lining system with a seepage load (to account for fluid
22 
head in the leachate collection system); seepage loads were based on results from the leachate
23 
system hydraulic analyses
24 
* 
Seismic Loading: self-weight of the lining system with seismic loading
25 
The results of the analyses show that the lining system is stable for the conditions analyzed and no
26 
anchorage forces are required to meet the minimum factors of safety (1.5 for dead load only; 1.3 for
27 
equipment and seepage loading). A minimum interface friction of 25 degrees and cohesion of 0 psf is
28 
required to meet the minimum acceptable factors of safety. The slopes are also considered to be stable
29 
under seismic loading, based on comparing the calculated yield acceleration and with the design
30 
acceleration values provided in the design criteria by CH2M HILL (September, 2002), using the hazard
31 
classification assigned to the overall facility.
32 
The critical interface friction values will be verified during construction to ensure that the system will be
33 
stable. The analyses and results are presented in full detail in Appendix C. I.a.
34 
5.1.2 
Earthwork Stability
35 
The earthwork stability analysis covered the following three cases:
36 
Excavation Case: This case covers the stability of the landfill slopes immediately after excavation and
37 
before placement of the lining system. Only static loading was considered since this is an interim
38 
configuration that will only exist for the construction period.
39 
Ramp Case: This case covers the stability of the landfill slopes and access ramp at the south end of the
40 
cell, including equipment loading on the ramps. Both static and seismic loading were examined, as the
41 
access ramps are expected to be in use for a period of at least 10 years.
42 
Dike Case: This case covers the stability of the perimeter dike (shine berm and access road) after
43 
construction of the dike and before final closure of the landfill.

5.1.3 
Waste/Fill Global Stability
13 
This analysis examined the following conditions:
14 
Phase I Full Build-Out: This case examined the stability of the waste mass in full build-out of the Phase
15 
1 waste cell. The critical stability examined was the waste sliding on the lining system. Both static and
16 
seismic loading conditions were examined.
17 
Final Configuration: This case examined the stability of the waste mass at the final configuration (entire
18 
IDF landfill completed) along the edge of the cover system. Only static loading conditions were
19 
examined, since this system is not being designed as part of the current effort.
20 
Interim filling conditions and the internal stability of the waste mass were not examined. The internal
21 
waste mass stability will primarily be a function of the filling methodology. Possible filling plans for the
22 
waste are currently being developed.
23 
For the analysis of the full build-out of Phase I, the critical interface strengths in the lining system were
24 
determined in the same way as for the veneer stability (regression analyses of existing and site specific
25 
testing data). A combination of peak and residual strengths were used, based on methodology currently
26 
being employed in the state of the practice. A final check was also made to confirm that the use of
27 
residual strengths in all locations resulted in a factor of safety greater than 1.0.
28 
The results show that the system is stable for the configurations analyzed and for the interface friction
29 
values available at the time of the analyses (FS greater than 1.5 in static loading and yield acceleration
30 
greater than the 10,000-year event). The system also has a FS greater than 1.0 for the case of residual
31

32

33

Strain on the liner was calculated using published values for the coefficient of linear thermal expansion

18 
length is measured from the top of the slope, where liner is anchored, to the toe of the 3H:IV side slope.

20 
expansion and strain on the liner. Additionally, a conservative temperature change of 40 degrees C

(104 degrees F) was used in the analysis.

The maximum liner strain was estimated to be less than 0.5 percent, based on a maximum temperature
23 
change of 40 degrees C (104 degrees F). The estimated maximum of slack in the liner on the side slope is
24 
8.6 inches. The corresponding amount of temperature induced stress is 566 psi. See Appendix C.5.a for

supporting calculations.

28 
at yield of 2,000 psi. Therefore, the maximum anticipated strains are well below the yield tensile strain
29 
and stress for the HDPE geomembrane, and temperature-induced strain will have no adverse impact on
30

5.6.3.2 Geosynthetic Clay Liner (GCL)
21 
The GCL underlying the geomembrane in the IDF landfill consists of processed sodium bentonite clay,
22 
sandwiched between two geotextile fabrics. Sodium bentonite is an ore comprised mainly of the
23 
montmorillonite clay mineral with broad, flat, negatively charged platelets that attract water, which
24 
hydrates the bentonite. The swelling provides the ability to seal around penetrations, giving the GCL its
25 
self-healing properties. A GCL product with Volclay-type sodium bentonite (manufactured by CETCO)
26 
is specified for installation at the landfill.
27 
The compatibility of GCL materials is usually demonstrated by permeating the material with leachate and
28 
then determining its hydraulic conductivity. Typically, solutions with high concentrations of
29 
contaminants or pure products are allowed to permeate a sample under confining pressure and the
30 
saturated hydraulic conductivity of the material is determined using ASTM methods such as ASTM
31 
D5084. A significant increase in saturated hydraulic conductivity (approximately one order of
32 
magnitude) for a sample permeated with leachate, compared with a sample permeated with water, would
33 
be an indicator of incompatibility.
34 
Based on review of the published studies (Ruhl and Daniel, 1997; Shackelford, et al., 2000; and EPA,
35 
1995), GCLs perform well unless exposed to high concentrations of divalent cations, very acidic or basic
36 
solutions, or solutions with a low dielectric constant (such as gasoline). The leachate expected at the IDF
37 
will have a pH of 9.2, which is a mid-range pH. The studies further demonstrate that, when confined
38 
under a higher normal load (greater than 2000 psf) or if water is the first wetting liquid (Daniel et al.,
39 
1997), GCLs will perform well when exposed to high divalent cation concentrations. The GCL for the
40 
IDF lining system is expected to confine under normal loads in excess of 2000 psf as soon as the first lift
41 
or waste is placed.
42 
No studies were identified that considered the long-term effects of radiation on the physical properties of
43 
GCL materials. Since long-term studies cannot be conducted, conservative radiation limitations have
44 
been employed. Low-hydraulic conductivity soils have been used at multiple DOE facilities containing
45 
radioactive waste. The only known potential adverse reaction that can occur with a GCL is high heat that
46 
could dry out the materials. The amount of radioactivity is expected to be low in the IDF landfill waste
47 
and will not generate a significant amount of heat that can desiccate the admix liner. Also, it is assumed
48 
that the ILAW packages will be cooled to ambient temperatures prior to placement with the cell.

It should be noted that the operations layer and drain gravel will provide a 3-foot buffer on the side slope
2 
and a 4-foot buffer between the liner system and waste for additional thermal protection, if needed.
3 
Sodium bentonite is the primary clay mineral in a GCL that produces the low hydraulic conductivity and
4 
high swell potential. Exposure of sodium bentonite to liquids containing concentrated salts (such as
5 
brines), or divalent cation concentrations (such as Ca++ and Mg++), reduces the swelling potential and
6 
increases its hydraulic conductivity. Concentrated organic solutions (such as hydrocarbons) and strong
7 
acids and bases can break down the soil, which also increases hydraulic conductivity. The physical
8 
mechanism that causes these changes is a reduction of the thickness, and related absorption capacity, of
9 
the diffuse double layer of water molecules surrounding the clay minerals. This results in an effective
10 
decrease in the volume of the clay, since the water molecules are not attracted to the clay particles.
11 
The GCL manufacturer allows the use of GCL with few restrictions on maximum chemical
12 
concentrations. Leachate concentrations for the IDF landfill (based on synthetic leachate from W025)
13 
have relatively high inorganics and dissolved salts. The W025 dissolved salt concentrations are above the
14 
manufacturers recommended concentration of 35,000 mg/L (see Table 5-3) (CETCO, 2001). As a point
15 
of reference, this concentration of dissolved salts is typical of seawater (USGS, 1989). However, the
16 
dissolved salt concentrations in the IDF leachate have been characterized as primarily sodium, and the
17 
synthetic leachate was comprised of entirely sodium salts, not the divalent cations such as Ca++ and
18 
Mg++, as assumed by the manufacturers. As such, the impact on GCL hydraulic conductivity should be
19 
less as compared to divalent cation solutions. Additionally, any effects of leachate degradation on the
20 
GCL would be minimized by hydration of the GCLs' sodium bentonite with relatively "fresh" water,
21 
allowing the GCL to swell initially and decrease hydraulic conductivity.
22 
The rationale for use of the GCL in the IDF landfill primary liner is to "deflect" leachate from defects or
23 
pinholes in the geomembrane over the bottom area and longer-term storage areas (such as the leachate
24 
sump trough), where leachate head potential is greatest. The main purpose of the primary GCL is to
25 
reduce the actual leakage rate into the LDS in the event of leak in the primary geomembrane (see
26 
Section 5.10 and Appendix C.10). The GCL is expected to contact leachate only in the event of a leak in
27 
the primary geomembrane. These leachate collection and storage areas are subject to flushing throughout
28 
the active life of the landfill due to phased development and fill sequence, resulting in a more dilute
29 
leachate in leakage areas prior to attaining maximum leachate concentrations. Based on these
30 
considerations, the GCL and landfill liner system approach should perform as intended under the
31 
anticipated conditions.

This was confirmed by W025 testing-there was an order of magnitude difference between samples with
14

15 
than concentrated leachate will be the first wetting liquid for the IDF admix liner.

13

14

15 
and is the standard model used for providing information necessary for the design of landfill systems.
16 
Estimates of the water balance components of the hydrologic cycle provided by HELP include
17 
precipitation, evapotranspiration, surface water runoff, vertical percolation, soil moisture storage, and
18 
lateral drainage in soil layers.
19 
The HELP model requires input of weather data, representing the conditions at the landfill location, soils
20 
data representing the various layers of cover soils, waste materials, and soils underlying the waste layers,
21 
and other design data used by the model for water balance calculations. A detailed description of the
22 
model and modeling inputs are included in Appendix C.7.

24

25

27 
under interim closure condition and Phase IV in the open condition with little or no waste present. The
28 
flows from this condition were used to size the LCRS collection piping and pump systems.
29 
Water balance components were taken directly from model output and a spreadsheet was used to calculate
30 
the volumes of leachate by multiplying the HELP output parameter by the area of the type of system
31 
modeled. For example, the lateral drainage estimated by the HELP model for the uncovered side slope
32 
condition in Phase IV development was multiplied by the total side slope area to determine the total
33 
volume of leachate from that area. A spreadsheet summarizing the estimated leachate flows is included in

Appendix C.7.

5.12.2.1 Crest Pad Building Foundation Analysis, Pipe Bracing and Winch
21 
The crest pad building foundation was analyzed as a concrete slab on an elastic foundation. The
22 
foundation was modeled with springs to model the vertical sub-grade reaction. The value of the vertical
23 
sub-grade reaction was provided by the geotechnical engineer. The applied loads and load combinations
24 
were input into Visual Analysis (version 4.0), a finite element program. The finite element analyses
25 
results include elastic settlement, moments, and shears values of the concrete slab. The results were then
26 
used to design slab depth and reinforcing.
27 
Load reactions from the pre-engineered metal building were estimated using hand calculations and
28 
applied onto the concrete slab at the corners of the slab. It is a reasonable assumption that the frame loads
29 
from the pre-engineered metal building will only occur at the corner of the building, since the size of the
30 
building will not require any intermediate framing.
31 
Loads and load combinations were used as required by TFC-ENG-STD-06, REV A. Performance
32 
category, PC-I was used as specified and applied as applicable for both wind, seismic, and load
33 
combinations requirements.
34 
In summary, the analyses results showed that an 8-inch thick slab sufficed with #5 reinforcing at 12-inch
35 
centers. The analyses results also showed that a 1 foot-10 inch edge thickening around the perimeter of
36 
the building would be sufficient. More detailed accounting of the analyses is presented in
37 
Appendix C.11.bl.
38 
The pipe bracing and support for the small diameter PVC (polyvinyl chloride) piping included both
39 
gravity as well as lateral load resistance, due to a seismic event. The governing piping support is assumed
40 
a 6-foot-tall cantilever support, with the piping load and 50 pounds of lateral load applied to the top of the
41 
support. The 50 pound lateral load was used in lieu of the calculated seismic load because the calculated
42 
seismic load was only 19 pounds. Using a 50 pound lateral load gives the pipe support system greater
43 
rigidity. Detailed calculations of the pipe supports are included in Appendix C.11.b2.
44 
The winch support was analyzed as a vertical cantilever that supports the winch and resists a total lateral
45 
load of 400 pounds.

5.12.2.2 Leachate Transfer Building Foundation Analysis
5 
As the leachate transfer building foundation is considered as a slab-on-grade, only hand calculations were
6 
performed. Foundation soil reactions were considered to be distributed linearly, then soil pressure
7 
distributions were applied to the concrete to calculated the moment and shear values for design of the
8 
concrete slab and reinforcing steel.
9 
Load reactions from the pre-engineered metal building were estimated using hand calculations and
10 
applied onto the concrete slab along the perimeter of the slab.
11 
Loads and load combinations were used as required by TFC-ENG-STD-06, REV A. Performance
12 
category, PC-1 was used as specified and applied as applicable for both wind, seismic, and load
13 
combinations requirements.
14 
In summary, the analyses results showed that the 2-foot-6 inch-thick slab with #6 bars at 12-inch centers
15 
will suffice and appears to be overdesigned. The 2-foot-6-inch thickness is not based on concrete strength
16 
requirements but more for frost depth cover, simplifying the ground forming, and reinforcing bending
17 
requirements. Detailed calculations of the analyses are presented in Appendix C.1 l.c.
18 
5.12.2.3 Leachate Tank Foundation Analysis
19 
The leachate tank foundation is considered to be a concrete ringwall, per AWWA D103-97. The tank
20 
gravity loads, including both water load and tank dead loads, were considered in the design of the
21 
ringwall.
22 
AWWA D103-97, Factory-Coated Bolted Steel Tanks for Water Storage is not listed in the TFC-ENG-
23 
STD-06, REV A. AWWA D100-96, Welded Steel Tanks for Water Storage, is listed; however, this
24 
standard does not apply, since the tank will be a bolted steel tank. Therefore, the tank will be designed
25 
per AWWA D103-97, Factory-Coated Bolted Steel Tanks for Water Storage.
26 
The analysis of the concrete ringwall and reinforcing is based on the hoop tension on the ringwall from
27 
the surcharge of the liquid weight on the soil within the ringwall. In summary, a 4-foot-6-inch-deep by
28 
1-foot-6-inch width ringwall with #7 at 12-inch-longitudinal reinforcing on each face of the ringwall will
29 
suffice. Detailed calculations of the analyses are presented in Appendix C.1 1.d.
30 
5.12.2.4 Truck Loading Station Foundation Analysis and Leachate Loading
31 
The Truck Loading Station foundation was analyzed as a concrete slab on an elastic foundation. The
32 
foundation was modeled with springs to model the vertical subgrade reaction. The value of the vertical
33 
subgrade reaction was provided by the geotechnical engineer. The applied loads and load combinations
34 
were input into Visual Analysis (version 4.0), a finite element program. The finite element analyses
35 
results include elastic settlement, moments, and shears values of the concrete slab. The results were then

38

WAC 173-303-665(2)(h)(i) requires that the IDF lining system have both a primary and secondary

18

22

26 
specified by Ecology guidance. Textured (roughened) geomembrane will be used to maximize shear

28

loads are presented in Section 5.5. Required material properties as a result of these analyses are included

in the technical specifications.

14 
placement with construction equipment and under the maximum static pressure from landfill contents at
15 
full waste height with final cover. A puncture analysis was performed to select a sufficiently thick

geotextile to protect the liner. This analysis included the maximum load from landfill contents and final

cover, expected construction vehicle ground pressures, and maximum drain gravel particle size listed in
18 
the technical specifications.

material. This material was selected because of its higher chemical resistance to the expected leachate

Stormwater Management
14 
The proposed stormwater system to be constructed just south of the south end of the Phase I excavation
15 
will intercept stormwater runoff from the area to the south for the 24-hour, 25-year storm event so that it
16 
will not flow into the Phase I excavation and will discharge the intercepted stormwater into the ground via
17 
infiltration. This system will consist of the south stormwater berm/ditch, two culverts, and the east and
18 
west infiltration areas. The berm will be two feet high above the existing ground surface. The minimum
19 
combined depth of the berm and ditch will be two feet. The ditch will be V-shaped with 3:1 side slopes.
20 
The culverts will be 18-inch-diameter, corrugated polyethylene pipe with smooth interior. Geotextile and
21 
quarry spalls will be placed around each end of the culverts to provide erosion protection. The east and
22 
west infiltration areas will have bottom lengths of 220 and 225 feet, respectively. Each of the infiltration
23 
areas will have a bottom elevation of 719 feet and a bottom width of 15 feet. In order to allow access for
24 
future maintenance into each of these infiltration areas, their north and south ends will be sloped at 15
25 
percent and surfaced with quarry spalls placed on a geotextile.
26 
The proposed stormwater system to be constructed at the south toe of slope within the Phase I excavation
27 
will intercept stormwater runoff from the unlined portions of the excavation for the 24-hour, 25-year
28 
storm event so that it will not flow into the active cells and will discharge the intercepted stormwater into
29 
the ground via infiltration. This system will consist of the excavation stormwater berm/ditch, a
30 
stormwater pipe, one catch basin, and the excavation infiltration area. There also will be a flow path
31 
along the south side of the access ramp that will continue along the south side of the flat area at the base
32 
of the access ramp and into the southwest corner of the excavation infiltration area. The south stormwater
33 
berm/ditch will slope to drain to the east. The combined depth of the berm and ditch will be two feet.
34 
The stormwater berm will be 2 feet high at its west end, and the corresponding depth of the ditch will be
35 
zero. The berm will gradually reduce in height as the depth of the ditch increases. The berm will end
36 
when the ditch depth reaches 2 feet. The ditch will be V-shaped with 3:1 side slope on the south and 2:1
37 
side slope on the north. The stormwater pipe will be 18-inch-diameter corrugated polyethylene pipe with
38 
smooth interior. Geotextile and quarry spalls will be placed around each exposed end of the stormwater
39 
pipe to provide erosion protection. The catch basin will be used to lower the elevation of the stormwater
40 
pipe so that there will be adequate cover over the pipe for protection against wheel loads. The infiltration
41 
area will have a bottom elevation of 678 feet, a bottom width of 15 feet, and a bottom length of 50 feet.
42 
In order to allow access for future maintenance into this infiltration area, the west end will be sloped at 15
43 
percent and surfaced with quarry spalls placed on a geotextile.

If the water builds up in the east or west infiltration area, it will eventually flow out of the north end of the
45 
infiltration area. The water would flow overland, north along the toe of the fill for the berm access road,

and continue generally northward.

containment area for the leachate in case of spillage. In order to maintain conformance with building

The discussion of waste placement in this plan is based on placement of the uniform height ILAW
3

4 
containers and for contact handle waste, but in general, the waste placement concept will be the same for
5 
all types of waste.

The configuration of IDF Phase I provides a height sufficient for four layers of ILAW packages, each
7

8

9 
of these four lifts. However, in some cases the LLW containers may exceed the lift height and, therefore,
10 
will not be completely covered by placement of the operations layer soil. In these cases, it may be
11 
necessary to mound cover soil around the individual projecting LLW containers to provide sufficient
12 
cover for shielding until they are completely covered by subsequent lifts.

Each lift will contain multiple ILAW package arrays that span the width of each cell. The packages will
14 
be placed in close-packet hexagonal arrays, with placement tolerance averaging 10 centimeters (4 inches)
15 
center to center. As the packages are placed in the cell, the array will proceed along the width of the cell.
16 
The earth cover will proceed shortly behind the advancing package array, the distance behind the front
17 
package limited by the repose slope of the fill soil. The array width (number of columns of packages)
18 
will be limited according to the amount of radiation generated by the total number of packages that can be
19 
exposed. The CDR indicates that even at some distance from the advancing array, the dose rate becomes
20 
a concern when the array approaches more than ten or twelve packages in width.
21 
Off-loading of the ILAW packages and other waste containers will take place in the cell. A standard,
22 
manually operated, rubber-tired crane will off-load packages, move temporary shielding walls (concrete
23 
blocks), and place the interstitial fill between the packages using a hopper. In the CDR, the total weight
24 
of the shielding bell, package grapple, load cell, hooks, and other rigging is estimated at 20 metric tons
25 
(23 tons). The crane, as identified in the CDR, will be a Grove GMK 5100, a 108 metric ton (120 ton),
26 
rough terrain rubber-tired crane with a telescoping boom and a maximum reach of 15 meters (50 feet),
27 
with a load of 20 metric tons (23 tons). Pad loads could exceed 55 metric tons (60 tons) when placing an
28 
ILAW package at the maximum allowable reach. Dunnage required under each outrigger pad of the
29 
crane for lifts of this size has been determined to be 60 square feet, when operating directly on the base
30 
operations layer at its point of minimum thickness over the bottom liner system. Dunnage requirements
31 
for subsequent lifts would be less, but have not been determined. Refer to Section 5.5.5 and Appendix

C.5.e of this Design Report for dunnage requirement calculations.

will be set up between the crane and transporter operations and the placed packages (CDR, Drawing No.
36 
ES-W520-BASE). With the 15-meter (50-foot) maximum reach of the crane, the shield walls will have to

be moved after every five rows of packages are placed. For a ten-package-wide-array, the wall will need
38 
to be relocated after fifty packages have been deposited, or about every eight days during Phase 1.

To prevent the crane crew from receiving a high exposure rate, a new shield wall will be erected before

previously placed shield wall from causing high dose rates to operations personnel. Even then, the

7.3 
Leakage Response Action Plan
3 
WAC 173-303-665(9) regulations require the owner of the operator of a landfill unit to have an approved
4 
Response Action Plan (RAP) before receipt of waste. The RAP is a site-specific plan that establishes
5 
actions to be taken if leakage through the upper (primary) lining system of a landfill exceeds a certain
6 
rate. The intent of the RAP is to assure that any leachate that leaks through the primary lining system will
7 
not migrate out of the landfill into the environment.
8 
A key element of the RAP is the ALR, a threshold value which triggers the responses described in the
9 
RAP, but below which no special actions are required. Because landfill liner systems have not yet been
10 
perfected, a small amount of leakage through the primary liner generally occurs, despite the use of best
11 
available materials, construction techniques, and QA procedures. (This leakage is collected by the LDS
12 
system and removed from the landfill.) Hence, the ALR is set at some level higher than normally
13 
expected leakage rates to serve as an indicator that the primary lining system is not functioning as
14 
expected. Exceeding the ALR may reflect serious failure of the primary lining system and indicates the
15 
need for investigation and possibly corrective action while the problem is still manageable.
16 
This RAP has been prepared in accordance with requirements of WAC 173-303-665(9). The
17 
requirements for determining the ALR are contained in WAC 173-303-665(8) and EPA guidance
18 
document, Action Leakage Rates for Leak Detection Systems (EPA 1992a).
19 
The following sections establish the ALR and discuss response actions to be taken if the ALR is
20 
exceeded.
21 
7.3.1 
Action Leakage Rate
22 
Section 5.11 provides a detailed discussion of the analysis to determine the ALR into the LDS for the
23 
IDF. Based on this analyses, the ALR for each IDF cell is 206 gallons per acre per day, or approximately
24 
1,800 gallons per day per cell (each cell area is approximately 8.5 acres). This value includes a factor of
25 
safety of 2 in accordance with EPA guidelines (EPA 1992b). It is also much lower than the LDS pump
26 
capacity. Details of the calculation are presented in Appendix C. 10.
27 
In accordance with WAC 173-303-665(8)(b), the flow rate used to determine if the ALR has been
28 
exceeded will be calculated as the average daily flow rate into the sump, expressed as gallons per acre per
29 
day (unless Ecology approves a different calculation). This calculation will be performed on a weekly
30 
basis during the active (operational) life of the landfill, and monthly after the landfill has been closed.
31 
Post-closure frequency may be reduced if only minimal amounts of leachate accumulate in the LDS
32 
sump. As outlined in WAC 173-303-665(4)(c)(ii), during post-closure monitoring, if the liquid level in
33 
the LDS sump stays below the pump operating level for two consecutive months, monitoring of the
34 
amount of liquid in the LDS sumps can be reduced to at least quarterly. If the liquid level in the LDS
35 
sump stays below the pump operating level for two consecutive quarters, monitoring of the amount of
36 
liquid in the LDS sumps can be reduced to at least semiannually. Pump operating level is defined as a
37 
liquid level approved by Ecology, based on pump activation level, sump dimensions, and level that
38 
minimizes head in the sump.
39 
7.3.2 
Response Actions
40 
WAC 173-303-665(9) lists several required actions if the ALR is exceeded. In the event that the ALR is
41 
exceeded, DOE will:
42 
* 
Notify Ecology in writing of the exceedance within 7 days of the determination.
43 
* 
Submit a preliminary written assessment to Ecology within 14 days of the determination, as to the
44 
amount of liquids, likely sources of liquids, possible location, size, cause of any leaks, and short-
45 
term actions taken and planned.
46 
* 
Determine, to the extent practicable, the location, size , and cause of any leak.

* 
Determine whether waste receipt should cease or be curtailed, whether any waste should be
2 
removed from the unit for inspection, repairs, or controls, and whether or not the unit should be
3 
closed.
4 
* 
Determine any other short-term and longer-term actions to be taken to mitigate or stop any leaks.
5 
Within 30 days after the notification that the ALR has been exceeded, submit to Ecology the results of the
6 
analyses specified in bullets 3, 4, and 5 of this section, the results of actions taken, and actions planned.
7 
Monthly thereafter, as long as the flow rate in the LDS exceeds the ALR, the owner or operator must
8 
submit to the regional administrator a report summarizing the results of any remedial actions taken and
9 
actions planned.
10 
If the ALR is exceeded, the DOE will submit the required notifications to Ecology, as stated above. The
11 
EPA will also receive copies of this confirmation.
12 
The leachate will be analyzed for chemical compounds and radionuclides. If the analytical results
13 
indicate that these constituents are present, and if the constituents can be traced to a particular type of
14 
waste stored in a known area of the landfill, then it may be possible to estimate the location of the leak.
15 
However, because the waste will meet land disposal restrictions, it will contain no free liquids and will be
16 
stabilized or solidified. In addition, the canister(s) or other type of waste package(s) may not undergo
17 
enough deterioration during the active life of the landfill to permit escape of its contents. For these
18 
reasons, it is possible that the leachate may be clean or the composition too general to indicate a specific
19 
source location.
20 
If the source location cannot be identified, large-scale removal of the waste and operations layer to find
21 
and repair the leaking area of the liner would be one option for remediation. However, this procedure
22 
risks damaging the liner. In addition, waste would have to be handled, stored, and replaced in the landfill.
23 
Backfill would need to be removed from around the waste packages to accomplish this. If the waste
24 
packages are damaged during this process, the risk of accidental release may be high. For these reasons,
25 
large scale removal of waste and liner system materials is not considered a desirable option and will not
26 
be implemented except as a last resort.
27 
The preferred options for remediation include covers and changes in landfill operating procedures. The
28 
preferred alternative will depend on factors such as the amount of waste already in the landfill, the rate of
29 
waste receipt, the chemistry of the leachate, the availability of other RCRA-compliant disposal facilities,
30 
and similar considerations. Hence, at this time no single approach can be selected. If the ALR is
31 
exceeded, potential options will be evaluated prior to selecting a remediation process. If necessary, an
32 
interim solution will be implemented while the evaluation and permanent remediation is performed.
33 
Examples of potential approaches include the following:
34 
* 
The surface of the intermediate soil cover over the waste could be graded to direct runoff into a
35 
shallow pond. The surface would then be covered with a discardable, temporary geomembrane
36 
(e.g., 30-mil PVC or reinforced polypropylene). Precipitation water would be pumped or
37 
evaporated from the pond and would not infiltrate the waste already in the landfill. Waste
38 
packages would be placed only during periods of dry weather and stored temporarily at other
39 
times. This type of approach would also be used, if necessary, to reduce leakage during the time
40 
immediately after the ALR was exceeded, while other remediation options were being evaluated.
41 
* 
If the landfill was nearly full, partial construction of the final closure cover might be an option.
42 
This would reduce infiltration into the landfill and possibly the leakage rate, if the cover were
43 
constructed over the failed area.
44 
* 
A layer of low-permeability soil could be placed over the existing waste, perhaps in conjunction
45 
with a geomembrane, to create a second "primary" liner higher in the landfill. This new liner
46 
would intercept precipitation and allow its removal.

A rigid-frame or air-supported structure could be constructed over the landfill to ensure that no
2 
infiltration occurred. Although costly, this approach might be less expensive than constructing a

new landfill.
4 
In general, the selected remediation efforts would be those that are easiest to implement, with more

trimming operations. Low spots or erosion rills shall be backfilled with structural fill as specified herein.

subgrade. The trimmed and watered surface shall be track-walked by D6-LGP dozer or equivalent with a
14 
minimum 4 passes to produce a firm and stable subgrade. Visual monitoring (no in-place density testing

is required) of the subgrade preparation on sideslopes will be performed by the CQA Certifying Engineer.

stable base. Allow for leachate piping and sumps or features as shown on the Drawings.

1.1 
Introduction
3 
This Construction Quality Assurance (CQA) Plan describes the quality assurance (QA) activities for
4 
constructing Phase I of the Integrated Disposal Facility (IDF) at the Hanford facility in Richland,
5 
Washington.
6 
1.1.1 
Applicable Units
7 
QA activities will be required during construction of Cell I of Phase I to certify that the following
8 
construction activities are performed in accordance with the construction documents:
9 
* 
Construction/preparation of foundation systems for liners.
10 
* 
Construction of dikes or embankments.
11 
* 
Construction of low-permeability soil liners.
12 
* 
Construction of geomembranes.
13 
* 
Construction of leachate collection and removal systems and leak detection systems.
14 
This CQA Plan has been prepared to describe the activities that will be performed during construction of
15 
the lining system, leachate collection and leak detection systems, and operation layer of Cell 1. This
16 
CQA Plan is intended to satisfy the regulatory requirements and guidance established in 40 CFR 264.19,
17 
the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) technical guidance document, Quality Assurance and
18 
Quality Control for Waste Containment Facilities (EPA 1993), and Washington Administrative Code
19 
(WAC) 173-303-335.
20 
This CQA Plan will be implemented by a CQA Officer (herein referred to as the CQA certifying
21 
engineer), a person familiar with EPA's technical guidance document, Quality Assurance and Quality
22 
Control for Waste Containment Facilities and this CQA Plan. The CQA certifying engineer will be
23 
supported by the number of CQA representatives necessary to implement the requirements in this CQA
24 
Plan and to document the work.
25 
1.1.2 
Scope
26 
This CQA Plan establishes general administrative and documentation procedures that will be applicable
27 
for selected activities of construction. With respect to responsibilities, personnel qualifications, and
28 
specific inspection and testing activities, this CQA Plan addresses only those activities associated with the
29 
soils, geosynthetics, and related liner and leachate collection system piping components for the IDF.
30 
The CQA requirements are divided into the following sections to provide quick access to CQA
31 
requirements for individual liner components:
* 
Soils CQA 
* 
Composite Drainage Net CQA
* 
Geosynthetic Clay Liner CQA 
* 
Polyethylene Pipe and Fittings CQA
* 
Geomembrane CQA 
* 
CQA Documentation and Certification
* 
Geotextile CQA 
* 
CQA Documentation and Certification
32 
1.2 
Project Organization
33 
This section describes the anticipated project organization for the IDF construction activities. The
34 
following subsections address the organizations involved in the construction, their respective roles in
35 
construction activities, and the methods of interactions between organizations.
36 
1.2.1 
Responsibility and Authority
37 
The organization chart for the IDF construction is shown in Figure 1-1. These personnel will be
38 
associated with two main entities that include the Tank Farm operating contractor and his agents and the
39 
construction general contractor and his personnel and/or subcontractors.

The project team consists of both full-time field personnel and part-time management personnel. The
2 
part-time management personnel will be onsite during the IDF construction periodically to monitor
3 
progress, attend meetings, resolve disputes, and ensure that the work is implemented in accordance with
4 
the construction drawings, technical specifications, CQA Plan, and the RCRA permit. The field
5 
personnel will consist of the key personnel onsite during construction. The solid lines on the organization
6 
chart represent project responsibilities such as scope, cost, and schedule. The dashed lines represent the
7 
functional responsibilities of staff for QA, design, and management. The responsibilities and reporting
8 
requirements for each project team member are described in the following sections.
9 
1.2.1.1 Project Team
10 
When the individuals identified below are designated to perform specific functions described in this CQA
11 
Plan, the reference to these individuals includes their designee or an alternate who can function on their
12 
behalf. The Department of Energy - Office of River Protection (DOE-ORP) Manager is the owner's
13 
representative and is responsible for project funding and overall project scope. The DOE-ORP manager
14 
and IDF project manager keep the regulatory agencies informed of IDF construction activities and
15 
progress.
16 
1.2.1.2 IDF Project Manager (PM)
17 
The IDF PM is an employee or agent of the Tank Farm operating contractor, has overall responsibility for
18 
the IDF construction, and interfaces with the DOE-ORP manager. The IDF PM directs the activities of
19 
the IDF project and field team staff, including the CM, design engineer, and the project engineer.
20 
Additionally, the IDF PM has overall responsibility for the achievement of quality. Functionally, the
21 
IDF PM reviews and approves quality assurance reports submitted by the IDF CQA certifying engineer.
22 
1.2.1.3 IDF Project Engineer
23 
The IDF project engineer is an employee or agent of the Tank Farm operating contractor and is
24 
responsible for providing technical support to the IDF project team. The IDF project engineer is
25 
supported by the design engineer for reviewing and/or preparing technical documents related to
26 
engineering design and analyses.

the IDF PM.

7 
The IDF design engineer is an employee or agent of the Tank Farm operating contractor is responsible for
8 
reviewing and/or preparing technical documents related to the IDF design and construction. The design
9 
engineer prepares the construction drawings, technical specifications, and the CQA Plan. The IDF design
10 
engineer reports to the IDF PM and supports the IDF project engineer.

1.2.1.7 IDF Construction Manager

The IDF CM is an employee or agent of the Tank Farm operating contractor and serves as the point of
14 
contact between the IDF construction general contractor and the IDF project team. All construction
15 
general contractor correspondence and direction flows through the CM. The CM oversees the daily
16 
construction field activities and is the onsite representative for the IDF PM.
17 
1.2.1.8 CQA Certifying Engineer
18 
The CQA certifying engineer is an employee or agent of the Tank Farm operating contractor who has the
19 
overall responsibility of implementing this CQA Plan and directly supervises the CQA monitor, field
20 
inspection team, and laboratory technicians. The CQA certifying engineer is responsible for preparation
21 
of an implementation plan that addresses how the CQA Plan is to be implemented, and how CQA work is
22 
to be performed, tracked, and coordinated, as well as how procedures outlined in this CQA Plan are to be
23 
followed. The implementation plan will be submitted to IDF project manager and CM for approval.
24 
Functionally, the CQA certifying engineer submits certified CQA reports to the IDF CM for review and
25 
approval by the IDF PM. The CQA certifying engineer is a registered professional engineer in
26 
Washington and has the authority to provide a certification letter that the IDF is constructed in accordance
27 
with the approved CQA Plan, the approved plans and specifications, and any approved changes. The
28 
CQA certifying engineer also has the authority and responsibility to stop work and recommend remedial
29 
actions to the IDF PM.
30

31 
Field inspectors are employees or agents of the Tank Farm operating contractor and report to the CQA
32 
certifying engineer. The field inspector's function is to perform testing and observations, in accordance
33 
with this CQA Plan and under the direction of the CQA monitor and CQA certifying engineer.
34 
1.2.1.10 
Soils Laboratory Technicians
35 
Laboratory technicians are employees or agents of the Tank Farm operating contractor and report to the
36 
CQA certifying engineer and provide the QA laboratory testing, required by this CQA Plan, as requested
37 
by the CQA monitor, and CQA certifying engineer.
38 
1.2.1.11 
CQA Surveyor
39 
The CQA surveyor will be an employee or agent of the Tank Farm operating contractor and will be a
40 
registered land surveyor in the State of Washington.

laboratory technician. The CQA monitor ensures that all CQA tests are performed in accordance with

this CQA Plan and accepted procedures.

1.2.1.13 
Construction General Contractor

The IDF construction general contractor is responsible for implementing the approved design by
8 
providing the necessary labor, equipment, materials, and all other resources necessary to construct the

IDF.
10 
1.2.1.14 
Construction General Contractor Site Supervisor
11 
The site supervisor is an employee or agent of the construction general contractor and is responsible for
12 
implementing the IDF construction activities. The site supervisor has overall responsibility for all
13 
construction activities related to the IDF, controls day-to-day construction tasks, and is the point of
14 
contact for construction general contractor field personnel. The site supervisor ensures the work is

progressing in accordance with approved construction contract documents and the approved schedule.

Construction Subcontractors
17 
Construction subcontractors include specialty companies, retained by the IDF construction general
18 
contractor, to perform specific work activities at the IDF such as earth moving, geosynthetic lining
19 
installation, piping, and building/tank installation. The construction subcontractors report directly to the
20 
construction general contractor site supervisor.

1.2.1.16 
Construction General Contractor Quality Control
22 
The construction general contractor provides a construction QC engineer who supports the site supervisor.
23 
The primary responsibility of the construction QC engineer is to ensure that the work is performed in
24 
accordance with the technical specifications and construction drawings. Specific duties of the
25 
construction QC engineer include activities such as preparing construction submittals, field
26 
documentation, and interfacing with the CQA certifying engineer.

1.2.2 
Project Meetings
28 
The various progress and status meetings that are anticipated to be held throughout the IDF construction
29 
are described below. The purpose of the meetings is to discuss work progress, planning, and other issues
30 
related to construction. A portion of these meetings can be dedicated to CQA issues, as necessary, to
31 
provide an opportunity for the CQA team to express concerns regarding quality, relay test results, and
32 
ensure good communication between all organizations involved in the construction of the IDF.
33 
1.2.2.1 Pre-Construction Meeting
34 
A pre-construction meeting will be scheduled prior to beginning construction activities for the IDF. At a
35 
minimum, the meeting will be attended by IDF staff including the PM, CM, project engineer, design
36 
engineer, as well as the construction general contractor site supervisor, and the CQA certifying engineer.

38

Reviewing the responsibilities of each organization.
40 
* 
Discussing the authority of agencies and project and field team members to order work stoppages.
41 
* 
Reviewing lines of authority and communication for each organization.
42 
* 
Providing each organization with all relevant CQA documents and supporting information.
43 
* 
Familiarizing each organization with the CQA Plan and its role, relative to the design criteria,
44 
plans, and specifications.

1.3 
Personnel Qualifications and Training
27 
This section describes the qualifications and training required for CQA personnel. All documentation
28 
relating to qualifications will be maintained with the project CQA records.
29 
1.3.1 
CQA Certifying Engineer
30 
The CQA certifying engineer will have landfill construction certification experience. The CQA certifying
31 
engineer will, at a minimum, be a registered civil professional engineer in good standing in the State of
32 
Washington, possess a bachelor's degree in civil or construction engineering, geotechnical engineering,
33 
engineering geology, or a closely related discipline, and have sufficient practical, technical, and
34 
managerial experience to direct successfully the CQA activities discussed in this CQA Plan. The CQA
35 
certifying engineer's qualifications will be documented by training records and a professional resume
36 
showing significant field experience in landfill construction and low permeability soil-bentonite admix

Rip and Tear Repair (Flat Surfaces)
11 
Rips or tears may be repaired by completely exposing the affected area, removing all foreign objects or
12

13 
place), with a minimum overlap of 12 inches on all edges.

15 
pound per lineal foot of edge, spread in a continuous 6-inch fillet.

17 
Damaged GCL material on slopes will be repaired by the same procedures as described above, however,
18 
the overlapped edges of the patch need to be wide enough to ensure the patch will keep its position during
19 
backfill or cover operations.

21

22 
inspected for any geotextile damage or bentonite loss. Damage will be repaired by the above-described
23 
procedure.

alternative measures must be taken to ensure the quality of the design dependent upon the degree of

damage.

4.2.4.7 Destructive Seam Testing
18 
Concept
19 
Destructive seam tests will be performed at selected locations. The purpose of these tests is to evaluate
20 
seam strength and integrity. Seam strength testing will be done as the seaming work progresses, not at
21 
the completion of all field seaming.
22 
Location and Frequency
23 
The CQA representative will select locations where seam samples will be cut out for laboratory testing at
24 
the frequency specified in the technical specifications (see Section 02661). In general, destructive tests
25 
will be located in non-critical areas, such as seam run-out areas or near three-panel intersections or other
26 
areas that will require a patch anyway. In addition, because extrusion welding may be limited on a daily
27 
basis, extrusion destructive samples may be welded after passing a trial seam on scrap material not used
28 
for construction. However, when significant lengths (greater than 100 feet) of seams or caps are extrusion
29 
welded, a destructive test of the weld will be taken.
30 
Control charts will be used to track the performance of each welding machine and technician to allow for
31 
biased sampling, according to performance. An upper control limit (UCL) will be established to identify
32 
statistically the sources of test failures. Machines and technicians whose failure rates exceed the UCL
33 
will then be identified and destructively tested at twice the original frequency (one per 250 feet of seam
34 
length) to better monitor their performance. Once the failure rate drops back into compliance with the
35 
UCL, the original testing frequency will be reinstated. Machines and technicians whose failure notes are
36 
below the UCL will be identified to decrease the original frequency, as approved by the CQA certifying
37 
engineer.
38 
The UCL is established based on the failure rate for all destructive tests plus three standard deviations
39 
with a ceiling of 3.5 percent. The ceiling is the maximum failure rate determined to be acceptable, as
40 
agreed upon jointly by the construction general contractor and CQA certifying engineer. The initial UCL
41 
will be calculated once a single machine or technician fails two destructive tests and will typically be
42 
updated daily with the most recent destructive testing results. Destructive tests tracking a failed
43 
destructive will not be included in the calculation of the failure rates.
44

4C.1. 
Leakage Response Action Plan
3 
WAC 173-303-665(9) regulations require the owner of the operator of a landfill unit to have an approved
4 
Response Action Plan (RAP) before receipt of waste. The RAP is a site-specific plan that establishes
5 
actions to be taken if leakage through the upper (primary) lining system of a landfill exceeds a certain
6 
rate. The intent of the RAP is to assure that any leachate that leaks through the primary lining system will
7 
not migrate out of the landfill into the environment.
8 
A key element of the RAP is the Action Leakage Rate (ALR), a threshold value which triggers the
9 
responses described in the RAP, but below which no special actions are required. Because landfill liner
10 
systems have not yet been perfected, a small amount of leakage through the primary liner generally
11 
occurs, despite the use of best available materials, construction techniques, and quality assurance
12 
procedures. (This leakage is collected by the LDS system and removed from the landfill.) Hence, the
13 
ALR is set at some level higher than normally expected leakage rates to serve as an indicator that the
14 
primary lining system is not functioning as expected. Exceeding the ALR may reflect serious failure of
15 
the primary lining system and indicates the need for investigation and possibly corrective action while the
16 
problem is still manageable.
17 
This RAP has been prepared in accordance with requirements of WAC 173-303-665(9). The
18 
requirements for determining the ALR are contained in WAC 173-303-665(8) and the Environmental
19 
Protection Agency (EPA) guidance document, Action Leakage Rates for Leak Detection Systems (EPA
20 
530-R-92-004).
21 
The following sections establish the ALR and discuss response actions to be taken if the ALR is
22 
exceeded.
23 
4C.1.1. Action Leakage Rate
24 
Section 5.11 provides a detailed discussion of the analysis to determine the ALR into the LDS for the
25 
Integrated Disposal Facility (IDF). Based on this analyses, the ALR for the IDF permitted cell is
26 
206 gallons per acre per day, or approximately 1,800 gallons per day per cell (each cell area is
27 
approximately 8.5 acres). This value includes a factor of safety of 2 in accordance with EPA guidelines
28 
(57 FR 19). It is also much lower than the LDS pump capacity. Details of the calculation are presented
29 
in Appendix C.10.
30 
In accordance with WAC 173-303-665(8)(b), the flow rate used to determine if the ALR has been
31 
exceeded will be calculated as the average daily flow rate into the sump, expressed as gallons per acre per
32 
day (unless Ecology approves a different calculation). This calculation will be performed on a weekly
33 
basis during the active (operational) life of the landfill, and monthly after the landfill has been closed.
34 
Post-closure frequency may be reduced if only minimal amounts of leachate accumulate in the leak
35 
detection system sump. As outlined in WAC 173-303-665(4)(c)(ii), during post-closure monitoring, if
36 
the liquid level in the LDS sump stays below the pump operating level for two consecutive months,
37 
monitoring of the amount of liquid in the LDS sumps can be reduced to at least quarterly. If the liquid
38 
level in the LDS sump stays below the pump operating level for two consecutive quarters, monitoring of
39 
the amount of liquid in the LDS sumps can be reduced to at least semiannually. Pump operating level is
40 
defined as a liquid level approved by Ecology, based on pump activation level, sump dimensions, and
41 
level that minimizes head in the sump.
42 
4C.1.2. Response Actions
43 
WAC 173-303-665(9) lists several required actions if the ALR is exceeded. In the event that the ALR is
44 
exceeded, the United States Department of Energy (DOE) will:
45 
* 
Notify Ecology in writing of the exceedance within 7 days of the determination.
Appendix 4C.5

WA7890008967
Integrated Disposal Facility
1 
* 
Submit a preliminary written assessment to Ecology within 14 days of the determination, as to the
2 
amount of liquids, likely sources of liquids, possible location, size, cause of any leaks, and short-
3 
term actions taken and planned.
4 
* 
Determine, to the extent practicable, the location, size, and cause of any leak.
5 
* 
Determine whether waste receipt should cease or be curtailed, whether any waste should be
6 
removed from the unit for inspection, repairs, or controls, and whether or not the unit should be
7 
closed.
8 
* 
Determine any other short-term and longer-term actions to be taken to mitigate or stop any leaks.
9 
* 
Within 30 days after the notification that the action leakage rate has been exceeded, submit to
10 
Ecology the results of the analyses specified in bullets 3, 4, and 5 of this section, the results of
11 
actions taken, and actions planned. Monthly thereafter, as long as the flow rate in the leak
12 
detection system exceeds the action leakage rate, the owner or operator must submit to the
13 
regional administrator a report summarizing the results of any remedial actions taken and actions
14 
planned.
15 
If the ALR is exceeded, DOE will submit the required notifications to Ecology, as stated above. The EPA
16 
will also receive copies of this confirmation.
17 
The leachate will be analyzed for Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) constituents. If the
18 
analytical results indicate that these constituents are present, and if the constituents can be traced to a
19 
particular type of waste stored in a known area of the landfill, then it may be possible to estimate the
20 
location of the leak. However, because the waste will meet land disposal restrictions, it will contain no
21 
free liquids and will be stabilized or solidified, except as allowed by Appendix 3A, section 1.2. In
22 
addition, the canister(s) or other type of waste package(s) may not undergo enough deterioration during
23 
the active life of the landfill to permit escape of its contents. For these reasons, it is possible that the
24 
leachate may be clean or the composition too general to indicate a specific source location.
25 
If the source location cannot be identified, large-scale removal of the waste and operations layer to find
26 
and repair the leaking area of the liner would be one option for remediation. However, this procedure
27 
risks damaging the liner. In addition, waste would have to be handled, stored, and replaced in the landfill.
28 
Backfill would need to be removed from around the waste packages to accomplish this. If the waste
29 
packages are damaged during this process, the risk of accidental release may be high. For these reasons,
30 
large scale removal of waste and liner system materials is not considered a desirable option and will not
31 
be implemented except as a last resort.
32 
The preferred options for remediation include covers and changes in landfill operating procedures. The
33 
preferred alternative will depend on factors such as the amount of waste already in the landfill, the rate of
34 
waste receipt, the chemistry of the leachate, the availability of other RCRA-compliant disposal facilities,
35 
and similar considerations. Hence, at this time no single approach can be selected. If the ALR is
36 
exceeded, potential options will be evaluated prior to selecting a remediation process. If necessary, an
37 
interim solution will be implemented while the evaluation and permanent remediation is performed.
38 
Examples of potential approaches include the following:
39 
* 
The surface of the intermediate soil cover over the waste could be graded to direct runoff into a
40 
shallow pond. The surface would then be covered with a discardable, temporary geomembrane
41 
(e.g., 30-mil PVC or reinforced polypropylene). Precipitation water would be pumped or
42 
evaporated from the pond and would not infiltrate the waste already in the landfill. Waste
43 
packages would be placed only during periods of dry weather and stored temporarily at other
44 
times. This type of approach would also be used, if necessary, to reduce leakage during the time
45 
immediately after the ALR was exceeded, while other remediation options were being evaluated.
46 
* 
If the landfill was nearly full, partial construction of the final closure cover might be an option.
47 
This would reduce infiltration into the landfill and possibly the leakage rate, if the cover was
48 
constructed over the failed area.
Appendix 4C.6

* 
A layer of low-permeability soil could be placed over the existing waste, perhaps in conjunction
2 
with a geomembrane, to create a second "primary" liner higher in the landfill. This new liner
3 
would intercept precipitation and allow its removal.
4 
* 
A rigid-frame or air-supported structure could be constructed over the landfill to ensure that no
5 
infiltration occurred. Although costly, this approach might be less expensive than constructing a
6 
new landfill.
7 
In general, the selected remediation efforts would be those that are easiest to implement, with more
8 
difficult or expensive options to be applied only if earlier approaches were not satisfactory.

PLC Standard Functions
20 
1. 
General -
PICS shall implement functions for the purpose of program standardization and
21 
minimum PLC application software capability. Functions may not be applicable to every program
22 
control loop or network.
23 
2. 
PLC Standard Function No. 1 -
Equipment Run Timers: For each equipment ON status input,
24 
track the runtime of the associated equipment item. Accumulate equipment runtime in tenths of
25 
hours using retentive timers with no timer reset due to equipment stoppage or power loss. Provide
26 
a command interface to allow reset or adjustment of equipment run time.
27 
3. 
PLC Standard Function No. 2A -
Equipment Failure Detection: Provide for each equipment item
28 
controlled by the PLC for which the PLC receives ON and AUTO or REMOTE status signals.
29 
Monitor for a fail condition when the unit is in the AUTO or REMOTE mode. A failure condition
30 
shall be activated when the unit is commanded by the PLC to run, and the PLC does not receive the
31 
unit's ON status signal after a 10-second delay period. When a failure condition is detected, inhibit
32 
the PLC run command to the unit. Reset the failure condition when the unit is taken out of AUTO
33 
or REMOTE mode.
34 
4. 
PLC Standard Function No. 2B -
Equipment Flow Failure Detection: Provide for each pump
35 
controlled by the PLC for which the PLC receives a PLC receives ON and AUTO or REMOTE,
36 
status and a PUMP DISCHARGE flow signal. Monitor for a fail condition when the unit is in the
37 
AUTO or REMOTE mode. A failure condition shall be activated when the unit is commanded by
38 
the PLC to run, and the PLC does not receive or maintain a positive flow value for a 10-second
39 
delay period. When a failure condition is detected, inhibit the PLC run command to the unit. Reset
40 
the failure condition when the unit is taken out of AUTO or REMOTE mode.
41 
5. 
PLC Standard Function No. 3 -
Analog Signal Scaling: Provide program logic to scale process
42 
analog signals to engineering units that correspond to the calibrated range of the field sensor. Store
43 
the scaled value in a PLC memory register for use in process control programming and for
44 
transmission to the OIU. Program PLC to monitor each analog input and ALARM in the event a
45 
process signal is out of the 4-2OmA range. A process signal out-of-range ALARM condition shall
46 
prevent associated process control from taking place.

PLC Standard Function No. 4 -
Analog alarms: Provide the capability to detect and annunciate
4 
alarms, such as high-high, high, low, and low-low for analog process signals. The PLC shall
5 
continuously compare the scaled process signal to a set-point value stored in PLC register memory.
6 
If the scaled process signal exceeds the alarm set-point, the PLC shall initiate an alarm signal to the
7 
OIU system and to external annunciation equipment as noted in the Process Control Loop
8 
Descriptions. The analog alarm function shall also have the following capabilities:
9 
a. 
Provide time delays on all alarm set-points. When the PLC detects the scaled process signal
10 
exceeding set-point, initiate the alarm delay timer. At the end of the time delay, activate the
11 
alarm.
12 
b. 
Unless specified in the Loop Functional Descriptions, all analog alarms shall be self-resetting.
13 
The PLC shall reset the alarm condition when the scaled process signal value is within the set-
14 
point value plus a 2 percent dead band.
15 
c. 
Where noted in the Loop Functional Descriptions, provide alarm ENABLE/DISABLE program
16 
logic that respond to commands from the OIU. Suppress the activation of alarms when
17 
commanded to the DISABLE mode.
18 
d. 
Provide program logic to receive, and store in PLC register memory, alarm set-point
19 
commands from the OIU.
20 
7. 
PLC Standard Function No. 5 -
Discrete alarms: Provide adjustable alarm delay timers on all
21 
discrete alarm input signals monitored by the PLC. Upon detection of the alarm condition, the
22 
PLC shall initiate the time delay. At the end of the time period, the PLC shall communicate the
23 
alarm condition to the OIU system and to external annunciation equipment as noted in the Process
24 
Control Loop Descriptions. The discrete alarm function shall also have the following capabilities:
25 
a. 
Unless specified in the Loop Functional Descriptions, all discrete alarms shall be self-resetting.
26 
The PLC shall reset the alarm condition when the alarm input signal resets.
27 
b. 
Where noted in the Loop Functional Descriptions, provide alarm ENABLE/DISABLE program
28 
logic that respond to commands from the OIU. Suppress the activation of alarms when
29 
commanded to the DISABLE mode.
30 
8. 
PLC Standard Function No. 7 -
Process Flow Totalizers: For all process flow signals provide
31 
program logic in the PLC to accumulate flow totals and flow total RESET. The totaled value
32 
stored in the PLC shall be transmitted to the OIU for display and historical logging. PLC shall
33 
increment flow total when pump ON status and minimum flow status is confirmed.
34 
9. 
PLC Standard Function No. 8 -
Pump Restart Time Delay: Provide adjustable delay timers in
35 
PLC program so as to prevent rapid restart of all pumps. An adjustable timer for each pump's
36 
AUTO start control logic, shall begin to countdown once a pump has stopped operating. PLC shall
37 
not execute AUTO start control logic for each pump until respective adjustable delay timer's
38 
accumulated value is equal to preset value of 30 seconds, except for Pumps P-205 and P-207,
39 
which will have a 10-second delay period.
40 
10. 
PLC Standard Function No. 9 -
Power Failure: Program PLC to prevent PLC from executing
41 
process equipment automatic control during a power failure condition.

1.0 
PURPOSE AND SCOPE
4 
The purpose of this management directive (MD) is to establish the requirements for standardized criteria
5 
for new graphic process displays (human-machine interfaces) that are being designed or acquired for
6 
process monitoring and control systems of CH2M HILL Hanford Group, Inc. (CH2M HILL) facilities
7 
and managed projects.
8 
The requirements of this MD are applicable to new monitoring and control system designs (Human-
9 
Machine Interfaces) for CH2M facilities and to projects that have not completed an Acceptance Test
10 
Procedure (ATP). Application of the MD requirements to existing human-machine interfaces systems
11 
and human-machine interfaces systems with a completed ATP will be determined, planned, and
12 
performed in accordance with the resolution of PER-2003-4039.
13 
2.0 
IMPLEMENTATION
14 
This management directive is effective on the date shown in the header and will remain in effect until a
15

3.0 
DIRECTIVE
17 
The following requirements that are based on the national standard ISA-S5.5-1985, "Graphic Symbols for
18 
Process Displays," are the Tank Farm Contractors (TFC) design requirement for new process monitoring
19 
and control systems (Human-Machine Interfaces).
20 
3.1 
General
21 
The following general symbol usage standards apply:
22 
1. 
The graphic process display will follow requirements specified in ISA-S5.5 standard.
23 
2. The use of outline and solid (filled) symbol forms to indicate status is as follows:
24 
* 
An outline symbol form indicates an off, stopped, or nonactive state.
25 
* 
A solid (filled) symbol form indicates an on, running, or active state.
26 
* 
Status designation by use of solid or outline forms are particularly applicable to the rotating
27 
equipment and valves and actuators. In depicting valve position, use solid to show open
28 
(material flowing or active) and outline to show closed (material stopped or nonactive).
29 
* 
A symbol may be partially filled or shaded to represent the characteristic of the contents of a
30 
vessel, e.g. level, temperature, etc.

The number of colors in one display should be limited to the minimum necessary (typically 4

or less) to satisfy the process interface objectives of the display.

Compatible color combinations should be used.

8 
blinking, and intensity coding to preserve communication with individuals having limited

color perception.
10 
* 
Colors are not to be used to indicate quantitative value.

5.0 GROUNDWATER MONITORING
2 
The Integrated Disposal Facility (IDF) will be an Resource Conservation and Recovery Act
3 
(RCRA)-compliant landfill (i.e., a double lined trench with leachate collection system). This chapter
4 
describes the groundwater monitoring plan for the IDF and addresses the requirements of RCRA, as
5 
described in 40 CFR 264, Subpart F, by reference of WAC 173-303-645(3). Figure 5.1 shows the
6 
location of the IDF and surrounding groundwater wells in the 200 East Area. This chapter is designed to
7 
meet final status detection-level groundwater monitoring requirements for the IDF. This groundwater
8 
monitoring plan is based on the application of a modified data quality objectives (EPA QA/G-4) process
9 
to a conceptual model, and the most recent evaluations of groundwater hydrology and chemistry at the
10 
site.
11 
This plan describes the characteristics of the waste to be disposed in the IDF and the site geology and
12 
hydrology used to design and operate the monitoring well network and to interpret the groundwater data.
13 
The historic groundwater chemistry from wells near the IDF site is provided. Much of the information
14 
pertaining to waste characterization is taken from HNF-4921 and that pertaining to hydrogeology from
15 
PNNL-1 1957, PNNL-12257, PNNL-13652, and PNNL-14029.
16 
The plan includes a description of network well locations, well construction, sample constituents, and
17 
sampling frequency for detection-level groundwater monitoring. Procedures for determination of
18 
compliance point groundwater quality also are included. Finally, this plan provides the basis for rapid
19 
development of a compliance monitoring plan if a validated exceedance of an indicator parameter is
20 
found. This plan controls initial baseline monitoring and subsequent detection level monitoring only for
21 
the IDF.
22
